pr_body:
This is reimplementation of NativeAOT ObjWriter in pure C# instead of depending on LLVM. It implements Mach-O, ELF, COFF object file emitter with DWARF and CodeView debugging information. Only x64 and arm64 targets are implemented to cover officially supported platforms (win-x86 code is present and lightly tested; linux-x86 code is present and incomplete, only serves as a test bed for emitting 32-bit ELF files if we ever need that).

Original object writer code is still present and can be used by setting the `DOTNET_USE_LLVM_OBJWRITER=1` environment variable.

**Thanks to @am11 for helping with testing and debugging this, @xoofx for making LibObjectFile which helped kickstart this project, @PaulusParssinen for tips about branchless U/SLEB128 size calculation, and all the people on the .NET team who helped push this forward!**

Fixes #77178

What is this, it is ilc.exe ??

> What is this, it is ilc.exe ??

Yes. It replaces the object file format writing of the ILC backend.
On that topic, dunno if ilc is already today using NativeAOT, but I assume that this PR should make it a lot more lightweight for this scenario, correct?

> On that topic, dunno if ilc is already today using NativeAOT, but I assume that this PR should make it a lot more lightweight for this scenario, correct?

ILC itself is published as NativeAOT executable. It's not compiled with the in-tree compiler though so it takes a little while till the bits propagate through the dependency pipeline into the SDK and back, but it's self-hosted.

It makes it slightly more lightweight in some ways. I expect the memory usage to reduce, although it's not trivial to compare with both the GC and native heap contributing to it. Performance measurements on smoke tests were favorable. It also simplifies the build process and dependency handling, especially for the full .NET source builds.
Yup, ilc is published as a NativeAOT app.
Is there any code/method left from the prototype that used existing NuGets? (Asking whether we need to add entry to `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.TXT`.)

> Is there any code/method left from the prototype that used existing NuGets?

The algorithm for `SizeOfULEB128` originally comes from https://android.googlesource.com/platform/art/+/ba257bc/runtime/leb128.h#101. It's two lines of code so that would very likely fall into fair use.

The only other thing that indirectly came from 3rd party sources were the constants in ElfNative.cs, MachNative.cs, and DwarfNative.cs. They were mostly taken from the specs where possible but few of them mirror the system headers.

Should the outputs of this and the LLVM object writer be identical byte for byte? I'm seeing different sizes on the same commit using each object writer for linux-x64.

> Should the outputs of this and the LLVM object writer be identical byte for byte?

TL;DR: No.

There are differences in the order of sections, string table order, temporary local symbols in symbol table, DWARF relocations (.debug_info -> .debug_info relocations were not correctly generated in the original ObjWriter), and DWARF compile unit headers.

Throughout the development I used a mode where I matched up the output more closely but it’s not an efficient thing to do and it was only useful for the initial debugging.

I switched later on to comparing the object files semantically through `readelf`, `objdump`, `dwarfdump` and other tools.

Aside from debugging information the linked output should be byte for byte identical.

I have looked through the code and it looks good. This is obviously a serializer that needs to follow all kind of quirks in corresponding formats and uses numerous constants and magic numbers, which would be hard to verify completely. Hopefully most of that are just copies/translations from the specs and references and thus correct. Also the tests are passing, so unwinding is working.

I have tested the debugging experience on Windows/Linux Release/Debug combinations and there is nothing that appears to be broken by the change. 

The statics/threadstatics natvis works too. 

![DebCapture](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/assets/8218165/dedb468a-ccba-4fe4-ae01-e8d79b8296dd)


**I do not see anything blocking, things look good and we can merge this.**

My only concern is the number of TODO/FIXME that are introduced. Also the difficulty to tell which of them can be fixed, should be fixed or perhaps are not really fixable. Some of the TODOs may match corresponding TODOs in LLVM, so those probably do not need fixing, for example.

I.E. which of the following are reasons to worry or can be picked up for fixing if someone has time?

```c
// TODO: Floating point

recordWriter.Write((ushort)0); // TODO: Attributes

// FIXME: Handle REGNUM_AMBIENT_SP

// TODO: Flags, CV_OFFSET_PARENT_LENGTH_LIMIT

// TODO: We are emitting .rela sections on x86 which is technically wrong.

. . .
```

We need to do something about TODOs while the code is fresh or soon noone will know which TODOs are actionable, how many of them remains etc..

I think, considering the size of the change, a TODO cleanup can be done as a separate change. 
Besides we may need to come up with some strategy for marking llvm things, x86 suggestions, vs. really actionable issues, which probably should not be TODOs in the code.

> // TODO: Floating point

We lack CodeView support for floating point registers - not a regression, should be an issue for follow-up.

> recordWriter.Write((ushort)0); // TODO: Attributes

I think I addressed those in CodeView. If I missed some I'll go back and update the code.

_UPD: I see, I missed the TODOs in `CodeViewSymbolsBuilder`. I'll revisit them and compare with the old ObjWriter._

> // FIXME: Handle REGNUM_AMBIENT_SP

Not a regression, tracking issue: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/77089

> // TODO: Flags, CV_OFFSET_PARENT_LENGTH_LIMIT

I'll double check this.

> // TODO: We are emitting .rela sections on x86 which is technically wrong.

Broadly speaking, the 32-bit support in NativeAOT has been broken for years for most of the platforms.

The linux-arm code didn't even compile for at least 2 years (Ref: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/96583). I wanted to have at least one ELF32 platform implemented to make sure that the generic code can handle it if anyone steps up to resurrect the ARM32 or x86 platform support. Given that not even CoreCLR supports linux-x86 I am open to removing the ELF/x86 ObjWriter code altogether. I added ELF/ARM32 instead to ensure that the ELF32 support doesn't fully bit rot.

There is rudimentary win-x86 support that's tested on a "Hello World" app with ZeroLib. It's just as good/bad as the old LLVM ObjWriter to support the "demo scene" type of apps that @MichalStrehovsky and few others do.

issue_context.title: Discussion: ObjWriter in C#
issue_context.body:
Let me start with a bit of a background. Last year I wrote [a library for manipulating MachO object files in C#](https://github.com/filipnavara/CodeSign) called Melanzana. Few weeks ago, I started doing some changes to the ObjWriter code and I found it to be quite suboptimal in terms of performance. As an exercise I wrote a [prototype of an ObjWriter replacement in C# for the MachO files](https://github.com/filipnavara/runtime/tree/objwriter2) based on my library. I later extended it to emit DWARF debugging information and ELF files as well through the [LibObjectFile library](https://github.com/xoofx/LibObjectFile/). Obviously, the code is not production ready and it is not on par with the current ObjWriter library but I wanted to gauge whether there would be an interest carrying this experiment forward.

What works?
- Producing MachO object files for osx-x64 and osx-arm64 targets
- Producing ELF files for linux-x64 and linux-arm64 targets
- Producing COFF files for win-x64 and win-arm64 targets
- DWARF debugging information for types, methods, variables, and line numbers
- CodeView debugging information for types, methods, variables, and line numbers

What doesn't work?
- No shared symbol (COMDAT) support for ELF
- No ARM32 and X86 support (NativeAOT doesn't properly support them anyway)

The obvious advantage of the approach is that the object writing libraries (whether it is LibObjectFile or Melanzana) are closer to the data model that the ILCompiler emits. That makes it more efficient at producing the raw section data, relocations, and symbol tables. The LLVM-based ObjWriter has high overhead (15%-30% of the whole compilation process in my tests). Some of the overhead can be reduced (eg. switching sections is expensive) but it usually comes at the cost of writing at least some part of the code in C#.

The disadvantage is that this is a lot of code and two external library references. Essentially, it's trading one dependency for another. While MachO and ELF formats are already part of the initial experiment the COFF one is not (all Windows targets).

There's also a middle way. Parts of the experiment can be reused to feed the data more efficiently into the current ObjWriter. For example, the unwinding sections (`__eh_frame`, `__compact_unwind`) could be produced completely in the managed code. That would avoid lot of overhead for section switching at minimal impact on portability (can be used only for specific targets).

The experiment also serves as a good testbed to quickly evaluate some space savings. Some little things I noticed:
- Non-primary LSDA frames contain relative pointer to main LSDA. This can be generated without symbols and relocations easily.
- Currently MachO produces `__eh_frame` data with 8-byte PC relative pointers. The linker can handle 4-byte ones as well so they can be used (as already done for ELF).
- ELF produces PLT relocations even within the same section. This seems to inhibit some optimizations and it's not recommended.

FWIW I am perfectly fine with ditching this as hack week project but I am also fine salvaging the good parts if it makes things fast(er) or improves the source build story.

> > No DWARF5 yet

The current ObjWriter DWARF 5 support is basically just writing different version number in the header. It doesn't use any of the new features and it's essentially useless. I could easily replicate that but there's really no point except for checking a checkbox.

The main benefit of DWARF 5 seems to be reducing the number of relocations. That's also non-issue for Mach-O since no relocations are necessary. Apple's linker doesn't copy DWARF to the final executable, instead it produces debug maps that reference the original DWARF data in the .o files. They can by collected by `dsymutil` into a bundled format but there's still no need for relocations.

I pushed a version with the memory usage optimization mentioned in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/77178#issuecomment-1282790964. A non-scientific benchmark with `Stopwatch` for generating COFF+CodeView currently looks like this:

Regardless, the work you've done is great! Very impressive.

The memory usage is smaller in the managed version although I didn't quite measure by how much.

It still builds the object file in memory but that's an implementation detail. For section content it uses a `Stream` wrapper around list of buffers. These buffers are the same buffers returned by `ObjectNode.GetData` and there's no further copying or slicing done on them. However, since the code works with `Stream` (and few specific -optional- optimizations) it's trivial to use temporary files, or memory mapped files if the output was too large to meaningfully fit into memory. That would be much harder to achieve with the LLVM ObjWriter code.

The LLVM ObjWriter currently slices the buffer from `ObjectNode.GetData` into tiny chunks to emit relocations, unwind codes, and debug line information. In the managed version all this can be easily avoided. Relocations that need to modify addend in data do so in-place. They are then collected into list which is already close to the output format (except for symbolic names not being resolved to symbol indexes yet; that needs to be done later - the symbol table may have sorting requirement and can only be emitted once all symbols were discovered). Unwind sections are built directly in their own separate memory stream in the respective format (DWARF EH or PDATA/XDATA). No slicing is necessary since we know the code offsets and we can bake them directly into the output format. That avoids the need to converts CFI code offsets into arbitrary code slicing, then having the ObjWriter emit the CFI codes at "current code offset", and reconstructing it back into the form that we had in the first place. Similar optimization applies to the debug line information.

Unlike LLVM we don't represent the relocations as symbolic expressions and we never go back to rewrite any of the data. Everything is generated in append-only fashion and then at the end merged into the final object file.

> If we end up doing enough work with LLVM otherwise (e.g., in Mono) it might be worth it to just try to improve LLVM instead. 

Mono's LLVM-AOT uses LLVM in a very different way than NativeAOT. Mono emits LLVM IR and then lets the toolchain do its thing through various layers (conversion, lowering, optimization, codegen etc.). While ObjWriter is a wrapper around a bunch of unexposed assembler APIs in llvm-project (the final/semi-final layer just before the object creation). So NativeAOT depends on a very small, private, surface area of llvm-project. 

If someone knows how ObjWriter works, they cannot use that particular knowledge to help troubleshoot issues with mono LLVM-AOT, and vice versa.

I'm going to leave this one open, but move it into the Future milestone, because I think there's a good chance that we stick with the objwriter for 8.0, since we have so much other work to do, and consider switching to a different implementation later.

@Thefrank, FYI - AFAIK, ELF sections don't differ between linux object files and that of FreeBSD; main thing which differs across various ELF OS is `E_IDENT` OS ABI magic bits, which will come in play if/when full linker is implemented in C# https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/92705#issuecomment-1848590647.

A quick scan over https://man.freebsd.org/cgi/man.cgi?elf(5) show it to be very close, if not exactly the same in most places as https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/elf.5.html. One note from the Linux manpage: 
> (Note: the *BSD terminology is a bit different.  There, Elf64_Half is twice as large as Elf32_Half, and Elf64Quarter is used for uint16_t.  In order to avoid confusion these types are replaced by explicit ones in the below.)

review_comments: What does our test coverage look like for big object vs. regular? I am wondering whether it would be a good idea to use big object unconditionally, even for smaller number of sections.

The big object files mainly kick in when the COMDAT sections are used to share method code. While some such sections can be produced in regular single file compilation, it's very limited occurrence and unlikely to hit the 65279 section limit of standard object file. The main trigger is the `--multifile` option (`IlcMultiModule` property in MSBuild), which changes the outcome of [this condition]( https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/fac60d0e972dd3f16ddc568573f2934c5fdc9acc/src/coreclr/tools/aot/ILCompiler.Compiler/Compiler/DependencyAnalysis/ObjectWriter.cs#L960-L967).

The test coverage on Windows is provided by the NativeAot runs with the `BuildNativeAotFrameworkObjects=true` parameter, and specifically by the `MultiModule` smoke test. We essentially get the normal objects tested by the regular smoke tests, and the big ones in the multi-file mode.

The downside of enabling big object files unconditionally is that the the format is not officially documented and many 3rd-party tools don't implement it, or implement it only partially. That makes analyzing the output at object file level cumbersome. Since the `IlcMultiModule` MSBuild property is not set by default and there's no official documentation for it, in vast majority of cases the big object files would not be encountered by the users.
`DW_CFA_..` are `byte` constants. No need to cast them.

[getRegName](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/fac60d0e972dd3f16ddc568573f2934c5fdc9acc/src/coreclr/jit/utils.cpp#L130-L148) and [its usage](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/fac60d0e972dd3f16ddc568573f2934c5fdc9acc/src/coreclr/jit/ee_il_dll.cpp#L866-L869).

For integer registers (` ICorDebugInfo::VLT_REG`), it uses the enum. For floating point registers (`ICorDebugInfo::VLT_REG_FP`, it takes the regnum as floating point register index that does not match what the JIT does.

Either way, this seems to be pre-existing problem.
How do we know that 4096 is enough?

The JIT blob format only encodes prologs. It’s limited to first 256 byte offsets, limited set of few opcodes, and not saving any register to stack more than once. I can redo the math but it’s essentially impossible for JIT to produce anything longer.

Alternatively, this would be easy to convert to `IBufferWriter<byte>` approach now.

(`DwarfFde` and `DwarfCie` code is the oldest part of the code which is why it used slightly different code style; they were part of an experiment with unwinding data I wrote during NativeAOT/macOS bringup)

`.LinkageName` vs. `.Name` mismatch?

This is intentional. Ref to old code: https://github.com/dotnet/llvm-project/blob/e80993c0649d5e949eb4ac23fe22290b4ecb7e66/llvm/tools/objwriter/debugInfo/dwarf/dwarfGen.cpp#L1001

Initially the DWARF tree is built with the debug names for both `Name` and `LinkageName`. The linkage name is then updated here to the actual mangled name matching the generated code.

a nit:

This name matches the one used in [native objwriter](https://github.com/dotnet/llvm-project/blob/e80993c0649d5e949eb4ac23fe22290b4ecb7e66/llvm/tools/objwriter/debugInfo/dwarf/dwarfGen.cpp#L880). Could we use a description in managed implementation instead of non-existent filename; such as,  `$".NET NativeAOT generated compile unit for '{outputFilename}'"` (by propagating `outputFilename=Path.GetFileName(objectFilePath)` from ObjectWriter to DwarfBuilder)?

According to the z/OS [docs](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/zos/2.1.0?topic=entries-source-file-name):
> If the source file is compiler generated, the name can be used to provides a description of the compiler generated file, and not necessarily a physical file name. 

which matches the scenario at hand.

e.g. dwarfdump output will read:
`Verifying unit: 1 / 116, ".NET NativeAOT generated compile unit for 'MyApp.o'"`
as opposed to:
`Verifying unit: 1 / 116, "il.cpp"`
This is extremely finicky bit, unfortunately. The main reason the attribute is even generated is to make Apple ld64 linker happy, and that linker expects valid file name / path in the attributes.
nit: Remove comment unless it's useful to have the assert

It's a bit of a double edged sword. The assert is useful to ensure that we do proper stacking of elements (ie. every Start is paired with End). Unforunately, the `Dispose` is also called when an exception is thrown, and in that case the assert would always trigger and make it impossible to see the exception.

I'm leaning towards deleting the line.
Where does this placeholder value come from?

It mimics what [LLVM uses](https://github.com/dotnet/llvm-project/blob/e80993c0649d5e949eb4ac23fe22290b4ecb7e66/llvm/lib/MC/MCCodeView.cpp#L59) (on multiple places). Some other LLVM tools do string based checks on it.

Empty file names have to be special-cased to prevent the UTF-8 string `\0` terminator being treated as the end of the file name list.
Just wondering - with the old ObjectWriter would we ever emit packed unwind info on ARM64?

No, we would not. It makes sense to open an issue to track whether we can do that. There’s already an issue for macOS compact unwinding and I assume the potential set of problems will be similar (JIT ABI matching the format, unwinding when in prolog).
